source.title: Efficient Generalization Improvement Guided by Random Weight Perturbation
source.authors: Tao Li; Wei Yan; Zehao Lei; Ying-Wen Wu; Kun Fang; Ming Yang; X. Huang

record.tranche_reason: Tests random weight perturbation training as a generalization-improvement method across image-classification architectures and datasets, including corruption and fine-tuning settings beyond the listed versions.
record.gate_note: Results comparing RWP, SAM, and SGD report test accuracy, training accuracy/loss, perturbation sensitivity, filter-norm distributions, and corruption performance. Cited prior-work findings are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses the premise that flatter minima generalize better to design RWP and evaluates its performance. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization-gap association or measure-ranking claim. Normalized landscape plots and filter-norm distributions measure related properties. None of V1–V6 or V8 receives a direct test.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase captures the authors' conclusion: jointly optimizing original and randomly perturbed losses improves accuracy, convergence, corruption robustness, and fine-tuning performance. Qualify the speed claim: measured iteration time falls by 44–46% relative to SAM using twice as many GPUs; RWP still uses two gradient evaluations and twice SGD's FLOPs.
record.recipe_differences: RWP combines the original loss gradient with a gradient from filter-wise random weight perturbations; it is compared with SGD and SAM rather than reproducing the original versions' interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, architecture, RWP balance coefficient α, perturbation magnitude γ, batch selection for gradient steps, training epoch budget, corruption severity, and use of original-loss gradient affect reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: RWP produces a wider flat region than SAM along the plotted normalized random direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RWP can broaden the measured loss landscape relative to SAM on ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10.

fits_no_version.finding: RWP produces more concentrated filter norms than SGD, with a stronger concentration effect than SAM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Filter-wise random perturbation training can promote more balanced filter norms.

fits_no_version.finding: RWP improves clean accuracy over SGD in the reported comparisons and is competitive with SAM, with larger advantages on ImageNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Joint optimization of original and randomly perturbed losses can improve image-classification accuracy under the tested recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: RWP performance depends on perturbation magnitude and gradient mixing; intermediate settings perform best.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Combining original and perturbed gradients with suitable perturbation strength improves RWP performance over its endpoint ablations.

fits_no_version.finding: Clean-trained RWP models perform better under the reported common corruptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RWP can improve corruption robustness without training on the corrupted evaluation data.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam-RWP improves reported accuracy over Adam in transformer fine-tuning and training from scratch.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RWP can improve transformer performance when added to Adam.

record.problems: The results are largely performance comparisons of RWP, SAM, and SGD rather than direct measurements of training-test gaps. Some figures are described without exact values. CIFAR trials use 3 independent runs; ImageNet results report no uncertainty. No random-label memorization, width threshold, or magnitude-aware sharpness-gap association is tested.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported accuracy comparisons were omitted. Figure-only point values for α, γ, corruption severity, or landscape curves were not reconstructed where the text did not state exact values.

untested.parts: No random-label fitting and held-out natural-label versus random-label comparison.
No width sweep identifying interpolation and subsequent test-error behavior.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison under matched tuning conditions.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison; large-batch training is proposed as future work.
No dropout intervention, training-set-size comparison, or joint dropout and weight-decay removal.
No magnitude-aware sharpness ranking of training–test error gaps among comparably fitted networks, and no comparison with norm- or margin-based measures.
No memorization-based example removal, random-removal control, or retraining comparison.

record.verdict_notes: States of cannot_determine indicate that these measures cannot establish a listed version, not that the reported accuracy improvements are unreadable. Own-method comparisons and hyperparameter-selection results should be retained as contextual findings rather than evidence for these versions. No omitted result directly tests a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or natural-label-versus-random-label generalization comparison.
No width sweep around or beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks or tests of local connectivity.
The study compares methods using SGD, and Adam in ViT and fine-tuning experiments, but does not test the claim about adaptive optimizers versus SGD under the specified tuning conditions.
No magnitude-aware sharpness comparison against norm- and margin-based measures; no test of correlation across a network family at similarly low training loss.
No removal of memorized examples or comparison against removing random examples.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Loss and accuracy along a normalized random weight direction for SAM- and RWP-trained models.
rows.measure: Training and test loss/accuracy landscape across weight perturbations
rows.value: RWP could obtain a wider flat region than SAM.
rows.note: The text describes wider flatness, but does not state a magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or a training-test gap ranking.
rows.check: Figure 2 shows a wider flat region along a normalized random direction, but does not establish a magnitude-aware perturbation-tolerance ranking against training–test error gaps at similarly low training loss.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared filter norm distributions for models trained by RWP, SAM, and SGD.
rows.value: RWP's filter norm distribution is much more concentrated than SGD's; SAM has a similar regularization effect, but RWP's is more obvious.
rows.note: This is a measured property proposed as a possible explanation for generalization gains, but the study does not measure whether it tracks the training-test gap.
rows.check: Filter-norm concentration is neither magnitude-aware sharpness nor its association with generalization gaps.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated CIFAR-10-trained methods on the most severe corruption level; averaged over 15 corruption types.
rows.baseline: SGD and SAM accuracies not numerically stated in Table 3 excerpt
rows.value: RWP consistently outperforms SAM by 3.0% on CIFAR-10-C.
rows.note: For this combination, the extracted table excerpt does not retain a row with per-model numbers; paper states the comparison in prose.
rows.check: Training was on clean CIFAR-10, with evaluation on CIFAR-10-C. Table 3 supplies exact accuracies: SGD 56.42%, SAM 58.22%, RWP 61.21%, a 2.99 percentage-point improvement over SAM. This robustness comparison tests no listed version.
